title: Linear slot machines
part: I: Geometry and mechanics in flat spacetime
one_line_summary: Introduces 1-forms as the dual partners of vectors (down-index objects pictured as stacks of surfaces), defines tensors as linear machines that eat vectors and 1-forms and return numbers, works out how components and bases transform so that contractions stay invariant, and cashes the formalism in by building the energy-momentum tensor of dust and reading its meaning by feeding an observer's 4-velocity into its slots.
role_in_book: Chapter 4 closes the flat-spacetime toolkit of Part I. Chapter 2 gave 4-vectors, the Minkowski dot product and observer-measured components; Chapter 3 gave coordinate transformations of basis vectors. This chapter adds the second kind of first-rank object (the 1-form), the general tensor with valence (m,n), index raising and lowering, and the tensor transformation law, so that Chapter 5 can generalize the metric and Part II can talk about covariant derivatives, Riemann curvature and the field equations. It also plants the energy-momentum tensor early as the future right-hand side of Einstein's equation, to be revisited in Chapter 12, and deliberately leans on the metric even though 1-forms do not need one; the metric-free, rigorous treatment of forms is postponed to Part V (Chapters 31-32).

assumed_background.topic: 4-vectors, basis vectors and the summation convention
Minkowski metric components diag(-1,1,1,1) and the dot product (eqn 2.15)
Component of a vector measured by an observer, X_0^obs = -X·u (eqn 2.38)
Transformation of basis vectors under a change of coordinates, with Lambda as a matrix of partial derivatives
Lorentz factor, length contraction and Lorentz transformations
Lagrangian mechanics and canonical momentum p = dL/d(qdot)
Matrix inverse, linear maps and dual spaces at an intuitive level
Dirac bra-ket notation and de Broglie matter waves
Pressure and shear stress in a continuous medium
Vector notation in electromagnetism as an example of efficient index-free notation

learning_objectives: Reader can explain why a vector at a point on a curved space lives in the tangent space at that point rather than in the space itself, using the Oxford-to-Durham example.
Reader can lower and raise indices with the Minkowski metric and its inverse, and state that X_0 = -X^0 while spatial components are unchanged.
Reader can describe up and down components geometrically in a non-orthogonal basis: up components from the parallelogram rule, down components from dot products with the basis vectors.
Reader can define a 1-form as a linear map from vectors to real numbers, expand it in basis 1-forms, and picture it as a stack of evenly spaced surfaces whose density measures its size.
Reader can use the duality relation <omega^nu, e_mu> = delta^nu_mu to evaluate a contraction as sigma_mu X^mu and to extract components by inserting basis objects into slots.
Reader can interpret physical quantities as 1-forms: wave phase difference as surfaces of constant phase pierced, E = -p(u) and n = -J(u) for an observer with 4-velocity u.
Reader can show that partially filling the metric, eta(v, ·), produces the 1-form with components v_mu, and connect this to index lowering.
Reader can write and justify the transformation laws for vector components, 1-form components, basis vectors and basis 1-forms, and prove that X_mu Y^mu is invariant.
Reader can define a tensor of valence (m,n) as a multilinear slot machine, build tensors with the outer product, extract components, and apply the tensor transformation law one factor per index.
Reader can argue that energy density picks up two Lorentz factors under a boost and hence belongs to a second-rank tensor.

Reader can construct T = J ⊗ p for dust, read off T^00, T^0i and T^ij as energy density, momentum density and stress, write the rest-frame matrices for dust and a perfect fluid, and interpret T(u,u), T(u,a) and T(u, ·) for an observer.
Reader can state why a tensor equation true in one frame is true in all, and why a scalar can be evaluated in whichever frame is most convenient.

teaching_approach.summary: An informal, picture-rich chapter that motivates a second first-rank object by asking what vectors must be paired with so that combining them yields a coordinate-invariant number. The authors first reach 1-forms through components (the metric absorbed into a vector gives down components), then recast everything in a single governing metaphor: tensors as slot machines with vector and 1-form slots and a crank that outputs a number. Geometry (tangent planes, stacks of surfaces pierced by arrows, parallel versus perpendicular projections) is paired with explicit index calculations in boxed examples, and physics examples (de Broglie phase, observer-measured energy and number density) keep the abstractions grounded. The chapter closes with a payoff: the energy-momentum tensor of dust, interrogated by inserting an observer's velocity into its slots.
narrative_arc: Motivating puzzle: following a straight arrow due North from Oxford leaves you above Durham, so vectors on a curved space must live in a flat tangent space at a point.

Motivating question: to form invariant numbers from vectors we need partner objects whose components transform oppositely; the bra-ket pairing of quantum mechanics is offered as a familiar precedent, and 1-forms are pictured as stacks of planes.

Component route (§4.1): absorb the metric into one vector of the dot product to define down components, then define the inverse metric and raising, and show geometrically what up and down components are in an oblique basis.
Reframe (§4.2): the metric becomes a two-slot machine eta( , ); valence (m,n) is introduced; vectors and 1-forms become one-slot machines whose mutual filling is the contraction <sigma, X>.
Core rule: the duality relation <omega^nu, e_mu> = delta^nu_mu turns contractions into sigma_mu X^mu and lets basis objects extract components.

Geometric and physical interpretation: contraction counts surfaces pierced, illustrated by wave phase; momentum and current 1-forms fed an observer's 4-velocity give minus energy and minus number density.
Bridge back to the metric: filling one slot of eta maps a vector to its 1-form, the geometric version of index lowering.
Consistency check (§4.3): require invariance of X_mu Y^mu to derive how down components transform, then show basis 1-forms transform like vector components; summarize all four laws.

Generalization (§4.4): arbitrary (m,n) tensors as slot machines, the outer product as slot-order bookkeeping, component extraction, the tensor transformation law, raising and lowering on tensors, and two corollaries on frame independence.

Payoff (§4.5): a gamma-squared argument shows energy density is part of a second-rank tensor; the energy-momentum tensor is built as J ⊗ p, its components interpreted as fluxes of 4-momentum, specialized to dust and a perfect fluid, and finally probed slot by slot with an observer's velocity.
signature_moves: The single overarching 'linear slot machine' metaphor, with cartoon machines that have labelled slots, a crank and a spout that emits a number.
Valence bookkeeping as an accounting rule: add the (m,n) of everything inserted and the machine, and a scalar results only when the totals match.
Introducing a new object twice: first as a component trick (absorbing eta into Y), then as a coordinate-free geometric object, with a margin warning that the first route is not the fundamental one.
Physical quantities defined by what an observer measures when their 4-velocity is inserted into a slot, with explicit minus signs from the metric signature.
Deriving a transformation law by demanding that a scalar stays a scalar, rather than postulating it.
Using index position itself as a mnemonic for transformation behaviour (down-index components move with down-index basis vectors).
Spoiler margin notes that point forward to where each object will matter (Ricci scalar, Einstein equation, Chapter 12).
Explicit preference for the slot-machine definition of a tensor over the coordinate-transformation definition, justified by the 'death by indices' remark.

sections.title: Chapter opening: vectors in tangent spaces and the need for 1-forms
sections.summary: Opens with the Oxford-Durham picture: an arrow tangent to the Earth at one city ends in the air above the other, showing that vectors belong to a flat tangent space attached at a point and that journeys on curved spaces are paths, not vectors. Recalls that vectors are coordinate-free objects expanded as X = X^mu e_mu. Introduces 1-forms (from Cartan's differential forms) with basis 1-forms omega^mu and down-index components, notated with a tilde. Explains the need: pairing two objects into an invariant number requires one whose components transform oppositely, just as bras pair with kets. Pictures a 1-form as evenly spaced planes whose density gives its magnitude, and announces the umbrella idea that tensors are linear slot machines producing scalars.
key_moves: A tangent arrow from Oxford overshoots the curved Earth, so vectors must be local objects living in the tangent space at a point.
Distinguish a path through a space from a vector between endpoints.
Motivate 1-forms by invariance: combining with vectors must give a scalar, so components must transform contragrediently.
Offer the bra-ket pairing as a precedent for objects living in a dual space.
Give the geometric picture of a 1-form as a family of parallel planes, with spatial frequency as magnitude.

sections.title: Dot products and down vectors
sections.summary: Starts from the Minkowski dot product eta_{mu nu} X^mu Y^nu and defines down components Y_mu = eta_{mu nu} Y^nu, so the dot product becomes a single up-down sum. Example 4.1 shows X·e_lambda equals X_lambda and, for diagonal Minkowski components, only the time component flips sign. The inverse metric eta^{mu nu} is defined and used to raise indices. Example 4.2 uses a non-orthogonal 2D basis to show that up components come from the parallelogram decomposition while down components come from dot products with the basis vectors, related by the inverse of a non-diagonal metric. The section ends by announcing that down components belong to a new object, the 1-form X̃ = X_mu omega^mu, while a margin note cautions that 1-forms do not actually require a metric.
key_moves: Absorb eta_{mu nu} Y^nu into a new object Y_mu so that X·Y = X^mu Y_mu.
Show X·e_lambda = X_lambda: a down component is a dot product with a basis vector.
Evaluate the lambda = 2 case explicitly to see that in Minkowski components X_i = X^i and X_0 = -X^0.
Define eta^{mu nu} by eta_{mu nu} eta^{nu lambda} = delta and write the dot product with two down components.
In an oblique basis contrast parallelogram (up) and projection (down) components and connect them via eta^{ij}.
Announce the 1-form X̃ = X_mu omega^mu as the home of down components.

sections.title: Vectors and 1-forms
sections.summary: Recasts the metric as a two-slot linear machine eta( , ) that outputs the dot product, calls it a (0,2) tensor and introduces valence (m,n). Vectors become (1,0) and 1-forms (0,1) tensors; a scalar results when the valences of machine plus inputs balance. The contraction <sigma, X> = sigma(X) = X(sigma) is defined, and with the duality rule <omega^nu, e_mu> = delta^nu_mu it reduces to sigma_mu X^mu. Example 4.3 extracts components by inserting basis objects. Example 4.4 uses de Broglie waves: the phase difference between two points is the contraction of the wave's 1-form (its surfaces of constant phase) with the separation vector, i.e. the number of surfaces pierced. Example 4.5 identifies the momentum 1-form (components from the Lagrangian) and the particle-current 1-form, which give -E and -n when fed an observer's 4-velocity, checked in the rest frame. The section closes by showing that filling one slot of the metric turns a vector into its 1-form.
concepts: contraction of a 1-form with a vector
component extraction by inserting basis objects
metric as a map from vectors to 1-forms
key_moves: Write eta(X,Y) = eta_{mu nu} X^mu Y^nu and state bilinearity (4.17).
Define valence and the balancing rule for producing a scalar.
Treat vector and 1-form symmetrically: X(sigma) = sigma(X) = <sigma, X>, with a margin caution that this symmetry fails for complex bra-kets.
Expand both objects in bases, use linearity, and apply <omega^nu, e_mu> = delta^nu_mu to get sigma_mu X^mu.
Extract X^mu = X(omega^mu) and sigma_mu = sigma(e_mu).
Interpret the contraction as counting planes pierced, via the phase of a matter wave.
Define physical 1-forms by the observer measurement they encode: p(u) = -E, J(u) = -n; verify in the rest frame where u = e_0.
Identify sigma·X = eta(sigma, X) = <sigmã, X> and conclude eta(sigma, ·) = sigmã.

sections.title: Transformations
sections.summary: Demands that the contraction X_{alpha'} Y^{alpha'} be invariant. Given that up components transform with Lambda^{alpha'}_mu = ∂x^{alpha'}/∂x^mu, the down components must transform with the inverse matrix ∂x^nu/∂x^{beta'}, and the product of the two matrices collapses to a Kronecker delta. Down components therefore transform like basis vectors. Example 4.6 multiplies the duality relation by transformation matrices to show that basis 1-forms transform like vector components. A margin note writes eqn 4.30 in components and gives the wave 1-form components k_mu = (-omega, k). The four transformation rules are collected in eqn 4.37.
concepts: transformation of basis vectors and basis 1-forms
key_moves: Posit X^{alpha'} = (∂x^{alpha'}/∂x^mu) X^mu and require X_{alpha'} Y^{alpha'} = X_mu Y^mu.
Use Lambda^nu_{alpha'} Lambda^{alpha'}_mu = delta^nu_mu to infer X_{beta'} = (∂x^nu/∂x^{beta'}) X_nu.
Observe that index position tracks transformation type: lower-index components and basis vectors transform alike, upper-index components and basis 1-forms transform alike.
Derive omega^{sigma'} = Lambda^{sigma'}_beta omega^beta by transforming both sides of the duality relation.

sections.title: Tensors
sections.summary: Defines a general tensor T as a linear machine with m 1-form slots and n vector slots, valence (m,n), and introduces the outer product ⊗ as a device that keeps track of slot order. Example 4.7 evaluates e_1 ⊗ e_2 on two 1-forms and the mixed tensor omega^2 ⊗ e_3 on a vector and a 1-form. Example 4.8 extracts components of a (3,1) tensor by inserting basis objects, expands the tensor in outer products of basis objects, and evaluates it on arbitrary inputs. The tensor transformation law is stated as one Jacobian factor per index, with the authors preferring the slot-machine definition. Example 4.9 writes the metric as eta_{mu nu} omega^mu ⊗ omega^nu, shows eta(v, ·) = v_nu omega^nu, and defines the (2,0) inverse metric. Indices on tensor components can be raised and lowered one at a time. Two corollaries close the section: tensor equality in one frame implies equality in all, and scalars have the same value in every frame. Margin notes introduce abstract index notation and warn against 'death by indices'.
concepts: component extraction by inserting basis objects
key_moves: Generalize from one-slot and two-slot machines to an (m,n) slot machine.
Use ⊗ so that each factor acts on its own slot, and evaluate products of basis objects on inputs via the duality rule.
Components of a tensor are its values on basis 1-forms and basis vectors; the tensor is components times outer products of basis objects.
Transform components with one ∂x'/∂x factor per up index and one ∂x/∂x' factor per down index.
Partially filling the (0,2) metric maps vectors to 1-forms; the (2,0) version maps 1-forms to vectors.
Argue frame independence by considering the difference tensor C = A - B, which vanishes identically.

sections.title: Energy-momentum tensor
sections.summary: Payoff section. For dust at rest the energy density is n_0 m; boosted, each particle's energy gains a gamma and length contraction raises the number density by another gamma, so energy density scales as gamma squared, the signature of a second-rank tensor. Recalling that the particle current J = n_0 u carries number density and particle flux, the authors argue that the flux of the 4-vector momentum must be a rank-two object and define (for now) T = J̃ ⊗ p̃ with components T_{mu nu} = J_mu p_nu, symmetric and convertible to T^{mu nu}. Example 4.10 evaluates T^{mu nu} = n_0 m u^mu u^nu, identifies T^00 as energy density, T^0i as momentum density or energy flux, T^ij as stresses, interprets T^{mu nu} as flux of p^mu across surfaces of constant x^nu, and gives rest-frame matrices for dust and an isotropic fluid with pressure. Finally Example 4.11 feeds an observer's velocity u and a direction a into the slots of T = rho_0 ṽ ⊗ ṽ to read off energy density (T(u,u) = nE), momentum density along a, energy flux along a, and the momentum-density 1-form T(u, ·). Margin notes preview the Einstein equation and the sign changes when time indices are raised.
concepts: flux interpretation of the energy-momentum tensor
key_moves: Count gammas: one from relativistic energy per particle, one from contraction of the volume, so energy density transforms with gamma squared.
Since particle number is a scalar its flux is a vector; momentum is a vector so its flux must be rank two.
Define T = J̃ ⊗ p̃ and write T^{mu nu} = n_0 m u^mu u^nu.
Interpret each block of the matrix physically and via flux of p^mu across constant-x^nu surfaces.
Specialize to dust at rest (only rho) and an isotropic fluid (diag(rho,p,p,p)).
Use raising with eta to show T^{0i} = -T_{0i} while diagonal entries keep sign.
Probe T with the observer's 4-velocity: T(u,u) = nE, T(u,a) = -n p(a), T(a,u) = -E J(a), T(u, ·) = -n p̃.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: A three-point summary restates 1-forms as plane stacks paired with vectors, tensors as linear slot machines, and the energy-momentum tensor as a symmetric rank-two object describing 4-momentum flux with T^00 the energy density. Eight exercises follow on proving tensor character, the Kronecker delta, invariant traces, basis vectors and 1-forms in curvilinear coordinates, derivatives of the invariant norm, and the relativistic Doppler effect from the wavevector.
key_moves: Condense the chapter into three take-home ideas.
Practice the transformation law on outer products, Kronecker deltas and traces.
Compute non-Cartesian basis vectors and basis 1-forms from coordinate relations.

concepts.name: tangent space
concepts.definition: The flat vector space attached to a single point p of a manifold, containing all vectors (directions and rates of change) at that point; vectors at p belong to it rather than to the manifold itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Through the Oxford-Durham picture: an arrow tangent to the Earth at Oxford points off the surface, so the natural home of that arrow is a flat plane touching the sphere at Oxford (R^2 touching S^2). Fig. 4.2 sketches a flat sheet T_pM touching a curved manifold at p.
concepts.notes: Only an intuitive picture here; the formal construction is in GA appC and Part V. The chapter itself then works in flat Minkowski spacetime, where the distinction is invisible.

concepts.name: manifold
concepts.definition: A space that looks locally like R^n and whose points (events, for spacetime) can be labelled by coordinates, but which may be curved globally.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the caption of Fig. 4.2 as the curved space whose points spacetime events occupy, with the caveat that the book usually avoids this vocabulary.

concepts.name: 4-vector
concepts.definition: A coordinate-independent geometric object with magnitude and direction, expanded in a basis as X = X^mu e_mu with upper-index components; in this chapter it is recast as a linear machine with one slot that accepts a 1-form.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 2 as an arrow, then reinterpreted as a (1,0) tensor X( ) whose slot is filled by a 1-form.
concepts.notes: Footnote 1 recalls that the squared length X^2 is agreed by all observers.

concepts.name: basis vectors
concepts.definition: A set of vectors e_mu, one per coordinate direction, in terms of which any vector is written as X^mu e_mu; their mutual dot products give the metric components.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapters 2-3; used with dot products to produce down components (X·e_lambda = X_lambda) and later paired with basis 1-forms through the duality relation.

concepts.name: Einstein summation convention
concepts.definition: An index appearing once up and once down in a term is summed over all its values (0 to 3 in spacetime) without writing the sum sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout from eqn 4.1; the chapter emphasizes that invariant sums pair one upper and one lower index.
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.3 prints the upper limit of the sum as 4; for four spacetime dimensions it should be 3.

concepts.name: Minkowski metric
concepts.definition: The metric of flat spacetime, with components diag(-1, 1, 1, 1) in inertial coordinates, used to form the invariant dot product of vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from eqn 2.15 in a margin note, then used as the tool that lowers indices and as the prototype (0,2) tensor.

concepts.name: scalar product
concepts.definition: The bilinear, coordinate-invariant number formed from two vectors with the metric, X·Y = eta_{mu nu} X^mu Y^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: The chapter's starting point: a familiar way of making a scalar from two vectors, which is then rewritten with down components and finally as the output of the metric slot machine.

concepts.name: scalar invariant
concepts.definition: A number built from tensors with all slots filled (all indices contracted); it takes the same value in every coordinate system, so it may be computed in whichever frame is easiest.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked at the outset as the reason 1-forms are needed, used as the constraint that derives the 1-form transformation law, and restated as a corollary at the end of §4.4 with the Ricci scalar as a forward example.
prerequisites: contraction of a 1-form with a vector

concepts.name: index lowering
concepts.definition: Contracting an upper index with the metric to produce a lower-index component, Y_mu = g_{mu nu} Y^nu (here eta); with Minkowski components this flips the sign of the time component only.
concepts.how_introduced: By absorbing eta_{mu nu} Y^nu in the dot product into a single down-index object; later reinterpreted as filling one slot of the metric tensor, and applied index by index to higher-rank tensors.

concepts.name: inverse metric
concepts.definition: The matrix inverse of the metric components, eta^{mu nu} with eta_{mu nu} eta^{nu lambda} = delta_mu^lambda; as a (2,0) tensor it takes two 1-forms and maps a 1-form to a vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined right after lowering so that the process can be reversed; for Minkowski components it is numerically the same matrix, a coincidence the margin note warns will not hold for most rank-two tensors.

concepts.name: index raising
concepts.definition: Contracting a lower index with the inverse metric to obtain the upper-index component, X^nu = eta^{mu nu} X_mu.
concepts.how_introduced: As the mirror image of lowering once eta^{mu nu} is defined; used in Example 4.2 with a non-diagonal metric and in footnote 22 to relate T^{mu nu} and T_{mu nu}.

concepts.name: contravariant and covariant components
concepts.definition: For a vector in a given basis, the up components X^i are the coefficients in X = X^i e_i (parallelogram decomposition), while the down components X_i = X·e_i are dot products with the basis vectors (perpendicular projections when the basis vectors have unit length); they coincide only for an orthonormal Euclidean basis.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.2 and Fig. 4.4 use a skewed 2D basis, drawing dashed lines parallel to the axes for X^1, X^2 and dotted perpendicular drops for X_1, X_2, then linking them with the non-diagonal inverse metric.
concepts.notes: In Minkowski spacetime with an orthonormal basis the only difference is the sign of the time component.

concepts.name: 1-form
concepts.definition: A coordinate-independent linear map that takes a vector and returns a real number; it is expanded as sigmã = sigma_mu omega^mu with lower-index components and can be pictured as a stack of evenly spaced parallel surfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the partner needed to build invariants with vectors, first reached through down components of the dot product, then defined as a one-slot machine, visualized as planes, and interpreted physically through wave phase, momentum and particle current.
concepts.notes: Footnote 5 stresses that 1-forms exist without any metric; the metric only provides a correspondence with vectors.

concepts.name: basis 1-forms
concepts.definition: The set of 1-forms omega^mu dual to the basis vectors, defined by <omega^nu, e_mu> = delta^nu_mu; geometrically, stacks of surfaces of constant coordinate.
concepts.how_introduced: Named alongside the 1-form expansion at the chapter opening, described geometrically as planes perpendicular to the coordinate axes, and fixed by the duality rule; their transformation law is derived in Example 4.6.
concepts.notes: The book writes basis 1-forms as bold omega without a tilde.

concepts.name: p-form (differential form)
concepts.definition: An antisymmetric tensor with p vector slots used in Cartan's differential geometry; a 1-form is the p = 1 case.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned to explain the odd name '1-form', crediting Élie Cartan.
concepts.notes: Developed properly in GA ch32.

concepts.name: dual space
concepts.definition: The vector space of all linear maps from a given vector space to the real numbers; 1-forms at a point live in the dual of the tangent space there.
concepts.how_introduced: Compared to the bra space of quantum mechanics, which is dual to the ket space; later tied to the tangent space by the duality relation and bridged by the metric.
concepts.notes: The term cotangent space is not used in the chapter.

concepts.name: Kronecker delta
concepts.definition: The symbol equal to 1 when its two indices are equal and 0 otherwise; the mixed form delta^mu_nu is a genuine (1,1) tensor with the same components in every frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the result of pairing basis 1-forms with basis vectors and as the product of a transformation matrix with its inverse; Exercise 4.2 asks whether the all-up and all-down versions are tensors.

concepts.name: dual basis relation
concepts.definition: The defining relation between basis 1-forms and basis vectors: the 1-form omega^nu returns 1 on e_nu and 0 on every other basis vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented, and highlighted in a shaded box, as the single most important rule for manipulating tensors, needed to evaluate a contraction once both objects are expanded in bases.

concepts.name: contraction of a 1-form with a vector
concepts.definition: The number obtained by inserting a vector into a 1-form's slot (equivalently the 1-form into the vector's slot), equal to sigma_mu X^mu in any basis; it requires no metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined with angle brackets to put vector and 1-form on an equal footing, computed via linearity and the duality rule, and pictured as the count of 1-form surfaces an arrow pierces.
concepts.notes: Footnote 7: the symmetry X(sigma) = sigma(X) is a choice valid for real quantities; bra-kets differ by complex conjugation.

concepts.name: multilinearity
concepts.definition: A tensor is linear in each slot separately: scaling an input scales the output, and the output for a sum of inputs is the sum of outputs.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated for the metric machine (4.17) and, in a shaded margin box, for the contraction; it is what allows expansion of inputs in bases.
concepts.notes: The chapter opening points to Section 4.3 for linearity, but it is actually stated in §4.2.

concepts.name: component extraction by inserting basis objects
concepts.definition: The components of any tensor are its outputs when each slot is filled with the corresponding basis vector or basis 1-form: a vector fed the basis 1-form omega^mu returns X^mu, a 1-form fed e_mu returns sigma_mu, and a (3,1) tensor fed three basis 1-forms and one basis vector returns the corresponding component.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.3 for vectors and 1-forms, extended in Example 4.8 to a (3,1) tensor and in Example 4.9 to the metric.

concepts.name: stacked-surfaces picture of a 1-form
aliases: bongs of a bell (MTW image, not used here)
concepts.definition: A visualization of a 1-form as a family of parallel, evenly spaced surfaces: closer spacing means a larger 1-form, the surfaces' orientation encodes its direction, and its value on a vector is the number of surfaces the arrow crosses.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the answer to 'if a vector is an arrow, what does a 1-form look like?' with Fig. 4.3, then made physical with surfaces of constant phase of a matter wave.
prerequisites: contraction of a 1-form with a vector
formulas: \langle\tilde\sigma, X\rangle = \text{number of surfaces of } \tilde\sigma \text{ pierced by } X
concepts.notes: The count must be signed (surfaces need an orientation) and can be fractional; the book does not say this.

concepts.name: wavevector 1-form
concepts.definition: The 1-form k̃ whose surfaces are the wave's surfaces of constant phase, so that its contraction with a displacement vector gives the phase difference; its components are k_mu = (-omega, k).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.4 first computes phase difference with the 4-vector k and a dot product, then offers the alternative of counting constant-phase surfaces; a margin note in §4.3 lowers the index to get the components.

concepts.name: de Broglie relation
concepts.definition: Every particle has an associated wave, with momentum proportional to wavevector, p = hbar k, and |k| = 2 pi / lambda; relativistically p^mu = hbar k^mu with k^mu = (omega, k).
concepts.how_introduced: As the physical setting of Example 4.4, with a margin biography of de Broglie.

concepts.name: 4-momentum
concepts.definition: The 4-vector p^mu = (E, p) = m u^mu of a particle; lowering gives p_mu = (-E, p).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in footnote 8 and used to build the momentum 1-form and the energy-momentum tensor.

concepts.name: 4-velocity
concepts.definition: The unit timelike tangent to a world line, u^mu = gamma(1, v); in the rest frame u = e_0, and its lowered form is u_mu = gamma(-1, v).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in footnotes 8, 10 and 23 and used as the observer's probe inserted into slots of 1-forms and of T.

concepts.name: momentum 1-form
concepts.definition: The 1-form p̃ = p_mu omega^mu of a particle, with components naturally given by the Lagrangian as p_mu = ∂L/∂(dx^mu/dτ); fed an observer's 4-velocity it returns minus the energy that observer measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.5, as the answer to 'which physical quantities are naturally 1-forms?', checked in the particle rest frame.

concepts.name: canonical momentum
concepts.definition: The derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to a generalized velocity; because it differentiates with respect to up-index velocities it naturally carries a down index.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited briefly in Example 4.5 as the source of the momentum 1-form components.
concepts.notes: The book does not explain why a derivative with respect to an up-index quantity yields a down-index object; Exercise 4.6 hints at the same pattern.

concepts.name: observer-measured energy
concepts.definition: The energy of a particle measured by an observer with 4-velocity u is E = -p̃(u) = -p_mu u^mu, the minus sign coming from the (-,+,+,+) signature.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.5, linked back to eqn 2.38 for observer components, tested in the particle rest frame where u = e_0 gives E = -p_0 = p^0; reused in §4.5 when probing T.

concepts.name: particle current 4-vector
concepts.definition: J = n_0 u for a swarm with rest-frame number density n_0; its time component is the number density n = gamma n_0 and its spatial components are particle fluxes. As a 1-form, J̃(u) = -n gives the density an observer with 4-velocity u measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.5 via an observer carrying a small permeable box through a dust cloud and counting particles; recalled in §4.5 as the model for thinking about fluxes.

concepts.name: metric as a map from vectors to 1-forms
concepts.definition: Inserting a vector v into one slot of the (0,2) metric leaves a machine with one empty vector slot, i.e. a 1-form, whose components are v_mu = eta_{mu nu} v^nu; the (2,0) inverse metric does the reverse.
concepts.how_introduced: At the end of §4.2 by noticing that <sigma, X> equals the dot product of X with the vector obtained by raising sigma's index, then confirmed component by component in Example 4.9.

concepts.name: tensor
concepts.definition: A coordinate-independent object that takes m 1-forms and n vectors as inputs and returns a real number, linearly in each input; its components in a basis are its values on basis 1-forms and basis vectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced at the opening as the umbrella for all ways of making numbers, exemplified by the metric machine in §4.2, then generalized with the cartoon of Fig. 4.6 in §4.4; the authors prefer this definition to the transformation-law one.

concepts.name: valence of a tensor
concepts.definition: The pair (m,n) counting a tensor's upper-index components (1-form slots) m and lower-index components (vector slots) n; a scalar results when the total up and down counts of a tensor and its inputs balance.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with the metric as a (0,2) tensor, then vectors as (1,0) and 1-forms as (0,1), with the balancing rule illustrated by (1,0)+(1,0)+(0,2) = (2,2).
concepts.notes: The book's (m,n) counts up then down indices; some texts reverse this or use 'rank' for m+n.

concepts.name: metric tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric (0,2) tensor that takes two vectors and returns their scalar product; in a basis eta = eta_{mu nu} omega^mu ⊗ omega^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: The first slot machine of the chapter, drawn as a cartoon in Fig. 4.5, later expanded in basis 1-forms in Example 4.9.
concepts.notes: Printed eqn 4.46 repeats the index mu in the second basis 1-form; it should be omega^nu.

concepts.name: coordinate transformation matrix
concepts.definition: The matrix of partial derivatives Lambda^{alpha'}_mu = ∂x^{alpha'}/∂x^mu relating two coordinate systems; its inverse is Lambda^mu_{alpha'} = ∂x^mu/∂x^{alpha'}, and their product is the Kronecker delta.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 3 at the start of §4.3; the placement of primed indices tells which matrix is meant.

concepts.name: transformation law for vector components
concepts.definition: Upper-index components transform with the forward Jacobian: X^{alpha'} = (∂x^{alpha'}/∂x^mu) X^mu.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the given from which the other laws follow.

concepts.name: transformation law for 1-form components
concepts.definition: Lower-index components transform with the inverse Jacobian, X_{beta'} = (∂x^nu/∂x^{beta'}) X_nu, exactly as basis vectors do, which guarantees that contractions are invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by demanding invariance of X_{alpha'} Y^{alpha'} given the vector law.

concepts.name: transformation of basis vectors and basis 1-forms
concepts.definition: Basis vectors transform like 1-form components, e_{beta'} = Lambda^alpha_{beta'} e_alpha, and basis 1-forms like vector components, omega^{beta'} = Lambda^{beta'}_alpha omega^alpha, so that X^mu e_mu and sigma_mu omega^mu are unchanged.
concepts.how_introduced: Basis-vector rule recalled from Chapter 3; basis-1-form rule derived in Example 4.6 by transforming the duality relation; all four rules summarized in eqn 4.37.
concepts.notes: Footnote 14: index position (down for 1-form components and basis vectors) signals shared transformation behaviour.

concepts.name: outer product
concepts.definition: The product A ⊗ B of tensors that forms a new tensor whose slots are A's slots followed by B's, with (A ⊗ B)(inputs) = A(its inputs) B(its inputs); slot order matters.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as notation that records slot order, demonstrated in Example 4.7 on e_1 ⊗ e_2 and omega^2 ⊗ e_3, then used to expand general tensors and to build T = J̃ ⊗ p̃.
concepts.notes: In eqns 4.58-4.60 the book keeps writing ⊗ between numbers after the slots are filled; there it is ordinary multiplication.

concepts.name: mixed tensor
concepts.definition: A tensor of valence (m,n) with both m and n nonzero, so its components have both upper and lower indices.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 16, illustrated by omega^2 ⊗ e_3 in Example 4.7.

concepts.name: tensor transformation law
concepts.definition: Tensor components transform with one forward Jacobian factor ∂x'/∂x for each upper index and one inverse factor ∂x/∂x' for each lower index; in coordinate-based treatments this is taken as the definition of a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after component extraction for the (3,1) example, with the authors expressing their preference for the slot-machine definition; practised in Exercises 4.1-4.3.

concepts.name: index-free notation
concepts.definition: Writing tensors as whole objects with empty slots, such as S( , , , ), rather than as arrays of components, to reduce index clutter and expose geometric meaning.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 17 argues for it with the 'death by indices' remark and the comparison with learning electromagnetism without vector notation.

concepts.name: abstract index notation
concepts.definition: A notation in which indices label slots rather than components (for example T^{ab}_c for a (2,1) tensor), with a separate alphabet such as Greek letters reserved for actual components.
concepts.how_introduced: Footnote 15 as a remedy for the fact that bold-symbol notation hides valence; the book does not adopt it.

concepts.name: frame independence of tensor equations
concepts.definition: If two tensors are equal in one coordinate system they are equal in all, because their difference is a tensor whose components all vanish and stay zero under any transformation.
concepts.how_introduced: One of two corollaries closing §4.4, justified both geometrically and via the difference tensor C = A - B.
concepts.notes: This is the reason laws of physics are written as tensor equations.

concepts.name: second-rank tensor
concepts.definition: A tensor with two slots in total, of valence (2,0), (1,1) or (0,2); its components form a 4x4 array and transform with two Jacobian factors.
concepts.how_introduced: In §4.5 as the kind of object whose components pick up two Lorentz factors, as energy density does; footnote 20 lists (2,0) and (0,2).
concepts.notes: Footnote 20 omits the mixed (1,1) case.

concepts.name: symmetric tensor
concepts.definition: A two-slot tensor whose output does not change when its two inputs are swapped, so its components satisfy T_{mu nu} = T_{nu mu}.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted for the energy-momentum tensor and used in footnote 27 to show that momentum density along a equals energy flux along a.
concepts.notes: J̃ ⊗ p̃ is symmetric only because for dust J and p are both proportional to the same 4-velocity; the book does not say so.

concepts.name: trace of a mixed tensor
concepts.definition: Summing the upper and lower index of a (1,1) tensor gives a scalar, S^mu_mu, invariant under coordinate transformations.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 4.3.

concepts.name: dust
concepts.definition: A continuum model of matter made of particles that do not interact and share a common velocity at each point, so it has energy density and momentum density but no pressure or other stresses in its rest frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening model of §4.5, with a margin note that astrophysicists meet a lot of it, and reused in Examples 4.10-4.11.

concepts.name: Lorentz factor
concepts.definition: gamma = (1 - v^2)^{-1/2} in units with c = 1, the factor by which energies and time intervals grow and lengths along the motion contract in a boosted frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in the gamma-counting argument for energy density.

concepts.name: length contraction
concepts.definition: A region at rest in one frame is shortened by a factor gamma along the direction of relative motion when measured in a frame where it moves.
concepts.how_introduced: Supplies the second gamma in the transformation of dust energy density: the same particles occupy a smaller volume.

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric second-rank tensor describing the density and flux of 4-momentum of matter; T^{mu nu} is the flux of p^mu across a surface of constant x^nu, so T^00 is energy density, T^0i momentum density (equivalently energy flux) and T^ij stresses. For dust it is J̃ ⊗ p̃ = rho_0 ũ ⊗ ũ.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the payoff of the formalism and the future source term of Einstein's equation: gamma-counting shows energy density needs a rank-two object, the flux of a 4-vector is argued to be rank two, T = J̃ ⊗ p̃ is defined for dust, its components interpreted, and it is interrogated with observer velocities.
concepts.notes: Defined 'for now' only for dust; general matter and conservation are in GA ch12. Printed component formula after 4.51 reads J_mu rho_nu, which should be J_mu p_nu.

concepts.name: flux interpretation of the energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: Component T^{mu nu} gives the amount of the mu-th component of 4-momentum crossing a unit surface of constant x^nu; a surface of constant time is all of space, so crossing it measures density.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 4.10, as a second reading of the dust components after the direct evaluation, organized into bullet points for the time-time, time-space and space-space blocks.

concepts.name: stress tensor
concepts.definition: The spatial block of the energy-momentum tensor: momentum flux, whose diagonal entries are pressures (normal stresses) and off-diagonal entries are shear stresses.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified in Example 4.10 as the space-space components.

concepts.name: perfect fluid
concepts.definition: Matter with energy density rho and isotropic pressure p and no shear or heat flow in its rest frame, where T = diag(rho, p, p, p).
concepts.how_introduced: Second simple example in Example 4.10, deduced from isotropy (no momentum density, no off-diagonal stress); detailed treatment deferred to Chapter 12.
concepts.notes: Footnote 24 warns that p here is pressure, not momentum.

concepts.name: Einstein field equations
concepts.definition: The field equations of general relativity, relating a curvature tensor of spacetime to the energy-momentum tensor of its contents.
concepts.how_introduced: Only as a schematic 'curvature equals mass-energy density' spoiler in footnote 18 to motivate the energy-momentum tensor.

concepts.name: Doppler effect
concepts.definition: The change in a wave's measured frequency between observers in relative motion, obtainable by Lorentz-transforming the wavevector 4-vector k^mu = (omega, k).
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 4.8 only: boost the wavevector 4-vector (omega, k) and read off the transformed frequency; Appendix E gives the boosted frequency as omega' = gamma(omega - beta k^x).

key_equations.meaning: Starting point: the invariant product of two vectors uses the metric components.
key_equations.symbols: eta_{mu nu} Minkowski metric components; X^mu, Y^nu vector components

key_equations.name: Lowering an index
key_equations.meaning: Definition of down components by absorbing the metric into one vector.
The dot product becomes one sum over an upper and a lower index.

key_equations.name: Down component as a dot product with a basis vector
key_equations.latex: X\cdot e_{\lambda} = X^{\mu} e_{\mu}\cdot e_{\lambda} = X^{\mu}\eta_{\mu\lambda} = X_{\lambda}
key_equations.meaning: Projecting onto a basis vector yields the lowered component.

key_equations.name: Explicit sum for one lowered component
key_equations.meaning: Writing out the implied sum for lambda = 2 shows which metric entries survive; with diagonal eta only eta_22 remains.
With diagonal Minkowski components only the time component changes sign on lowering.

key_equations.name: Inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Defines eta^{mu nu} as the matrix inverse of eta_{mu nu}.

key_equations.name: Raising an index
key_equations.meaning: The inverse metric restores up components from down components.
Dot product written purely with down components and the inverse metric.

key_equations.name: Vector in a skewed basis
key_equations.meaning: Up components are the coefficients of the parallelogram decomposition along non-orthogonal basis vectors (Fig. 4.4).

key_equations.name: Up and down components in an oblique basis
key_equations.latex: X_j = X\cdot e_j,\qquad X^i = \eta^{ij}(X\cdot e_j),\qquad X^1 = \eta^{11}X_1 + \eta^{12}X_2
key_equations.meaning: In a non-orthogonal basis down components are projections and up components are recovered with the non-diagonal inverse metric.

key_equations.name: 1-form expansion
key_equations.meaning: Down components are the components of a 1-form in the basis of basis 1-forms.

key_equations.name: Metric slot machine
key_equations.meaning: The metric as a two-slot machine returning the dot product (expanded for diagonal components).

key_equations.name: Linearity of the metric
key_equations.meaning: The machine is linear in each slot.

key_equations.meaning: Bilinearity of the pairing, used to expand both arguments in bases.

key_equations.name: Contraction notation
key_equations.meaning: Inserting a vector into a 1-form or a 1-form into a vector gives the same number.
Linearity pulls components out, leaving pairings of basis objects.

key_equations.name: Duality relation
key_equations.meaning: Basis 1-forms and basis vectors are dual; the most important rule for tensor manipulation.

key_equations.name: Contraction in components
key_equations.meaning: A 1-form on a vector is the up-down sum of components: no metric needed.

key_equations.name: Extracting components
key_equations.meaning: Feed basis 1-forms to vectors and basis vectors to 1-forms to read off components.

key_equations.name: Plane-wave amplitude
key_equations.latex: \psi(x) = A e^{i\phi} = A e^{i k\cdot x} = A e^{i p\cdot x/\hbar}

key_equations.name: 4-dimensional phase difference
key_equations.meaning: In Minkowski space the phase difference includes the time part with a minus sign.

key_equations.name: Phase as surfaces pierced
key_equations.meaning: The wave 1-form's constant-phase surfaces counted along the separation vector give the phase difference.

key_equations.name: Geometric meaning of contraction
key_equations.latex: \langle\tilde\sigma, X\rangle = (\text{number of planes of } \tilde\sigma \text{ pierced by } X)
key_equations.meaning: General geometric reading of the pairing.

key_equations.name: Energy from the momentum 1-form
key_equations.meaning: Inserting an observer's 4-velocity into the momentum 1-form gives minus the energy that observer measures; component form p_mu u^mu = -E.

key_equations.name: Number density from the current 1-form
key_equations.meaning: Inserting an observer's 4-velocity into the particle current 1-form gives minus the measured number density; J_mu u^mu = -n.
key_equations.symbols: n number density measured by O_u

key_equations.meaning: Contracting a 1-form with a vector equals the dot product of the vector with the raised-index version of the 1-form.
key_equations.symbols: sigma = sigma^nu e_nu vector with raised components

key_equations.name: Metric maps vectors to 1-forms
key_equations.meaning: Filling one slot of the metric yields the corresponding 1-form (index lowering, geometrically). The component version is in the margin.

key_equations.name: Vector component transformation
key_equations.meaning: Up components transform with the forward Jacobian.
key_equations.symbols: primed indices refer to the new coordinates

key_equations.name: 1-form component transformation
key_equations.meaning: Down components must transform with the inverse Jacobian.

key_equations.name: Invariance of the contraction
key_equations.meaning: The two Jacobians cancel, so the up-down sum is a scalar.
Multiplying the duality relation by the transformation matrices in turn.

key_equations.name: Basis 1-form transformation
key_equations.meaning: Basis 1-forms transform like vector components.

key_equations.name: Summary of transformation rules
key_equations.meaning: The four rules: index position determines which Jacobian is used.

key_equations.name: Abstract index contraction (margin)
key_equations.meaning: Roman indices label slots, not components, and do not imply summation.
key_equations.symbols: a, b, c abstract slot labels

key_equations.name: Outer product of basis vectors on 1-forms
key_equations.meaning: Each factor of an outer product acts on its own slot.

key_equations.name: Mixed outer product
key_equations.meaning: A mixed tensor takes a vector in one slot and a 1-form in the other.

key_equations.name: Components of a (3,1) tensor
key_equations.meaning: Components are outputs on basis objects.

key_equations.name: Tensor expanded in a basis
key_equations.meaning: A tensor equals its components times outer products of basis vectors and basis 1-forms.

key_equations.name: Evaluating a tensor on inputs
key_equations.meaning: Output is the full contraction of components with input components.

key_equations.name: Tensor transformation law
key_equations.meaning: One Jacobian factor per index, forward for up and inverse for down.

key_equations.name: Metric in basis 1-forms
key_equations.meaning: The metric as a (0,2) tensor; eta(e_alpha, e_beta) = eta_{alpha beta}.

key_equations.name: Partially filled metric
key_equations.meaning: Explicit check that one filled slot of the metric produces the 1-form with lowered components.

key_equations.name: (2,0) metric
key_equations.meaning: Inverse metric as a tensor taking two 1-forms; maps 1-forms to vectors.

key_equations.name: Raising and lowering tensor indices
key_equations.meaning: The metric moves indices one at a time on any tensor.

key_equations.name: Energy density of moving dust
key_equations.meaning: One gamma from energy per particle, one from length contraction of the volume: energy density needs a rank-two tensor.

figures.label: Fig. 4.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Durham lies 337 km due North of Oxford; a straight line heading North from Oxford ends roughly 9 km above Durham because the Earth curves away (curvature exaggerated). The caption jokes that the same holds going South from Durham.
figures.visual_description: A thick black arc, stippled on its underside, sweeps from the lower left up to the upper right to represent a greatly exaggerated slice of the Earth's surface; the words 'Planet EARTH' are written along the inside of the arc. The label OXFORD marks a point on the arc about half way up. A straight bold arrow starts at Oxford, tangent to the arc, and runs to the upper right, ending with its head above the surface. A short dotted vertical line drops from the arrowhead down to the arc at the label DURHAM, showing the gap between the tip of the tangent arrow and the destination on the ground.
figures.what_it_teaches: A vector at a point is tangent to a curved space and does not lie in it; displacements between distant points on a curved space are paths, not vectors.

redesign.idea: A 3D globe with a flat tangent plane attached at a chosen city. The learner draws a straight tangent arrow of adjustable length and heading and sees it lift off the sphere, while a great-circle path of the same length stays on the surface. A readout shows the height of the arrow tip above the ground, approximately d^2/(2R).
redesign.interaction: Drag the base point, rotate the heading, slide the length (Oxford-Durham preset 337 km) and a radius slider to shrink or grow the planet; the height gap and tangent plane update live, and the gap shrinks to zero as the length becomes small compared with R.

figures.label: Fig. 4.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Vectors live in the tangent space T_pM at a point p of a (generally curved) manifold M, not in M itself.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn sketch of a curved, dotted surface like the side of a hill, labelled 'Manifold M' at the lower right. Resting on the surface and touching it at one point is a flat quadrilateral sheet drawn in perspective and labelled T_pM. On the sheet a point p is marked and a short arrow labelled X runs from p across the sheet. Shading under the sheet suggests it sits just above the curved surface except at p.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each point of a manifold has its own flat vector space of possible directions; vector operations happen there.

redesign.idea: A bumpy 3D surface with a tangent plane that follows the cursor. Vectors drawn at a point stay in that point's plane, and moving the point shows that tangent planes at different points are different spaces.
redesign.interaction: Click to place p; drag within the plane to draw X; move p and watch the plane re-orient, with a toggle to show two tangent planes at once to stress they cannot be added naively.

figures.label: Fig. 4.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: A 1-form pictured as a family of planes; its value on a vector X is the number of planes the arrow pierces.
figures.visual_description: Three identical hand-drawn rectangular sheets stacked in perspective, parallel and evenly spaced, each with hatched shading on its edge. A bold arrow labelled X enters from below the lowest sheet at the lower left, passes up through all three sheets (drawn dotted where hidden) and emerges above the top sheet, its head at the upper right.
figures.what_it_teaches: A 1-form has a geometric picture of its own, complementary to an arrow; contraction is counting crossings, so denser sheets mean a bigger 1-form and a longer or better-aligned arrow gives a bigger number.
concepts: contraction of a 1-form with a vector

redesign.idea: A 2D or 3D stack of oriented surfaces with numbered levels, and a draggable arrow. A live counter shows the signed, fractional number of surfaces crossed, which matches sigma_mu X^mu computed from components shown alongside.
redesign.interaction: Adjust the 1-form's components (spacing and tilt of the planes) and drag the arrow's tip; the crossing count, component sum and a 'positive/negative/zero' indicator update, including the case of an arrow lying within a plane (zero).

figures.label: Fig. 4.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Geometry of up (contravariant) and down (covariant) components in a skewed basis.
figures.visual_description: Two basis directions from a common origin: e_1 pointing horizontally to the right and e_2 slanting steeply up and to the right. A solid arrow X runs from the origin to a point between them. Dashed lines from the tip of X drawn parallel to each axis meet e_1 at a tick labelled X^1 and e_2 at a tick labelled X^2, completing a parallelogram. Dotted lines from the tip dropped perpendicular to each axis meet e_1 at X_1, further right than X^1, and e_2 at X_2, further along than X^2.
figures.what_it_teaches: Up components come from decomposing X along the axes (parallelogram rule) while down components come from orthogonal projections (dot products with basis vectors); they differ whenever the basis is not orthonormal.

redesign.idea: An interactive oblique-basis plane where both constructions are drawn simultaneously, with a live metric matrix g_ij = e_i·e_j and its inverse, and numeric up and down components that satisfy X_i = g_ij X^j.
redesign.interaction: Drag the tips of e_1, e_2 (angle and length) and of X; the parallelogram and perpendicular feet move, the matrices update, and when the basis becomes orthonormal the two sets of ticks merge.

figures.label: Fig. 4.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The metric as a slot machine eta( , ): insert two vectors, turn the handle, and a number (their dot product) comes out.
figures.visual_description: Cartoon of a boxy machine held together with corner bolts. On its front face sit two tall dark slot openings side by side, each with the small word 'vector' printed above it, and the word INSERT lettered underneath the pair. A crank handle projects from the left side with a curved arrow showing it being turned. A horn-shaped spout rises from the upper right and an arrow labelled 'number' comes out of it. Faint maker's-plate lettering decorates the top and bottom edges.
figures.what_it_teaches: A (0,2) tensor is a machine with two vector slots whose output is a scalar, linear in each slot.
